q: Adequate breathing and they need oxygen, versus apneic or inadequate. Which pair?

opts.t: Non-rebreather if adequate; bag if apneic or inadequate
opts.why: R/R/Q picks the device. Adequate plus need oxygen = NRB. Not enough air = BVM.

opts.t: Bag if adequate; non-rebreather if apneic
opts.why: Those are swapped.

opts.t: Cannula for both
opts.why: A cannula is not the test default, and it cannot ventilate.

opts.t: CPAP for both
opts.why: CPAP is for alert wet-lung patients who still breathe.

q: Unconscious, 18 breaths a minute, good chest rise. Which device?

opts.t: Non-rebreather to raise the percent
opts.why: Unconscious does not automatically mean bag them. Rate, rhythm, and quality decide.

opts.t: Bag them only because they are out
opts.why: 18 and good rise can still be adequate.

opts.t: Cannula at 1 liter
opts.why: If they need oxygen, the test default is a non-rebreather.

opts.t: CPAP even if they cannot follow commands
opts.why: Unconscious is a CPAP no.

q: Any mask on the face. What flow?

opts.t: 10 to 15 liters per minute
opts.why: Every face or trach mask is 10-15. Under 10 is a straw that suffocates.

opts.t: 1 to 6 liters per minute
opts.why: That is the cannula range.

opts.t: 2 to 4 liters per minute
opts.why: That is a common cannula play, not a mask.

opts.t: Under 10 liters per minute so they are not flooded
opts.why: Under 10 on a mask is the problem.

q: Why is it called a non-rebreather?

opts.t: Flaps let exhale out and seal on inhale so exhaled air is not breathed back in
opts.why: Non-rebreather = not rebreathing exhaled air.

opts.t: It has no reservoir, so they rebreathe room air only
opts.why: It has a reservoir. The flaps stop rebreathing.

opts.t: The valves are popped off on purpose
opts.why: Popping the valves off makes a partial rebreather.

opts.t: It runs at 1 to 6 liters
opts.why: A mask runs 10-15.

q: Nasal cannula numbers?

opts.t: 1 to 6 liters per minute, about 24 to 44 percent
opts.why: 1 L is about 24%. 6 L is about 44%. Room air is 21%.

opts.t: 10 to 15 liters per minute, about 90 to 95 percent
opts.why: That is the non-rebreather range.

opts.t: 1 to 6 liters per minute, 100 percent if sealed
opts.why: 100% is a sealed bag.

opts.t: 10 to 15 liters per minute, about 24 to 44 percent
opts.why: 24-44% is the cannula percent, not a mask flow.

q: Thinking of turning a cannula to 6 liters. What is the next thought?

opts.t: They probably already need a non-rebreather
opts.why: 6 liters whistles and dries the nose. If they need that much, think NRB.

opts.t: Stay at 6 forever because the test loves a cannula
opts.why: The registry rarely wants a cannula as the pick.

opts.t: Drop to under 10 on a mask instead
opts.why: A mask is 10-15, not under 10.

opts.t: Switch to CPAP for any 6-liter thought
opts.why: CPAP is a wet-lung tool, not a 6-liter bump.

q: Partial rebreather. How is it made, and what percent?

opts.t: Pop the non-rebreather side valves off; about 80 to 90 percent; still 10 to 15 liters
opts.why: Still a mask, so still 10-15. Book use is hyperventilation / panic later.

opts.t: Add extra valves; about 24 to 44 percent; 1 to 6 liters
opts.why: Valves come off, and that percent/flow is a cannula.

opts.t: Leave the valves on; 100 percent; 1 liter
opts.why: Valves on is a non-rebreather. 100% is a sealed bag.

opts.t: Use a colored adapter; invent the printed liters
opts.why: Colored adapters are Venturi. Printed numbers were not to be invented.

q: Venturi mask on the ambulance?

opts.t: Not an EMS carry; long-term percent control; read the adapter that is already on
opts.why: Do not invent color liters. Interfacility: match what is already on.

opts.t: Everyday first-line mask at 1 to 6 liters
opts.why: It is not stocked as a first-line EMS mask.

opts.t: The test default for any hypoxia
opts.why: The test default is a non-rebreather.

opts.t: Required on every D tank
opts.why: They do not carry it.

q: No trach mask in the bag. They breathe adequately through a stoma. What goes over the hole?

opts.t: A non-rebreather over the stoma at 10 to 15 liters
opts.why: Functionally a mask. Still need adequate breathing.

opts.t: A cannula in the nose at 1 liter
opts.why: The hole is the stoma, not the nose.

opts.t: A Venturi with invented color numbers
opts.why: Do not invent Venturi liters.

opts.t: CPAP because any hole gets pressure
opts.why: CPAP is not the stoma-cover move.

q: Need oxygen now, only a D tank on its side. Humidified oxygen?

opts.t: Give dry oxygen. A water jug on a laid-down D tank spills
opts.why: Humidify on an upright wall meter if a jug is there. Need oxygen now: give dry.

opts.t: Lay the jug on the D tank and wait
opts.why: It spills. They still need oxygen.

opts.t: Withhold oxygen until a wall meter is found
opts.why: Need oxygen now means give dry.

opts.t: Switch to CPAP to skip the tank
opts.why: CPAP still uses tank pressure.

q: Bag indication, flow, and percent if the seal is tight?

opts.t: Apnea or inadequate rate or volume; 10 to 15 liters; 100 percent
opts.why: Tight seal, no room-air leak. Seal is the job.

opts.t: Adequate but hypoxic; 1 to 6 liters; 24 to 44 percent
opts.why: That is a cannula, and adequate hypoxic is a non-rebreather.

opts.t: Apnea; under 10 liters; 21 percent
opts.why: A bag is 10-15, and a tight seal is 100%.

opts.t: Any unconscious patient; 2 liters; 80 to 90 percent
opts.why: Unconscious plus good rise can be a non-rebreather. 80-90% is a partial rebreather.

q: Adult with a pulse who needs to be breathed for. What rate?

opts.t: One breath every 6 seconds, which is 10 a minute
opts.why: Adult vent rate is 1 every 6 seconds = 10/min.

opts.t: One breath every 2 to 3 seconds, which is 20 to 30 a minute
opts.why: That is child and infant.

opts.t: 12 to 20 breaths a minute to match normal
opts.why: They get 100% and more volume, so 10 a minute, not 12-20.

opts.t: 40 shallow breaths to match a panic rate
opts.why: Do not match 40. Keep about 10 good breaths.

q: Child or infant who needs to be breathed for. What rate?

opts.t: One breath every 2 to 3 seconds, which is 20 to 30 a minute
opts.why: Child and infant: 1 every 2-3 s = 20-30/min. Same 10-15 liter flow.

opts.t: One breath every 6 seconds, which is 10 a minute
opts.why: That is the adult rate.

opts.t: A different liter flow than an adult mask
opts.why: Peds NRB, cannula, and BVM use the same LPM as adult. Kids get faster breaths, not different flow.

opts.t: One breath every 15 seconds
opts.why: 15 is not a bag interval.

q: How hard is a bag squeeze?

opts.t: Gentle, about 1 second, just until chest rise, then stop and count
opts.why: Not a blast. Count out loud so the hand waits.

opts.t: Hard and fast until the bag is empty
opts.why: Hard and fast stacks air and drops blood pressure.

opts.t: Half a bag, no look at the chest
opts.why: Stop at rise. Half a bag is not a known size.

opts.t: Match 40 shallow breaths if they have any
opts.why: Time with their inhale if they have one, but keep about 10 good adult breaths.

q: Bag too fast and too hard. What stacks?

opts.t: Air in the stomach, high chest pressure, blood pressure drops, pulse can go
opts.why: Gastric distension plus squeezed heart and vessels. Adrenaline is the usual cause.

opts.t: Only a dry nose from a 6-liter cannula
opts.why: That is a cannula problem, not a bag blast.

opts.t: Only a better seal
opts.why: A blast is not a better seal.

opts.t: Only a rise in residual volume that helps them
opts.why: Stacked pressure hurts the pump.

q: Apneic adult with no pulse. What replaces the 1-every-6-seconds-only plan?

opts.t: CPR; adult 30 compressions and 2 breaths this hour
opts.why: No pulse = CPR, not stand-alone 10 breaths a minute.

opts.t: Keep 1 breath every 6 seconds and skip compressions
opts.why: No pulse means compressions.

opts.t: CPAP because they cannot follow commands
opts.why: Arrest is a CPAP no. They need a bag and CPR.

opts.t: A cannula at 1 liter during compressions
opts.why: A cannula is not CPR.

q: Home 1-liter cannula, called for difficulty breathing, still adequate. What bump?

opts.t: Own assessment; if they need a lot, bump to a non-rebreather
opts.why: Home flow is not the scene plan. Adequate plus need a lot = NRB.

opts.t: Leave the home 1 liter because it is already on
opts.why: The scene assessment decides.

opts.t: Bag them only because they called
opts.why: Adequate means raise the percent, not take over.

opts.t: Start CPAP for any home-oxygen call
opts.why: CPAP needs the wet-lung, alert, pressure-ok picture.

q: Main CPAP patient on a question?

opts.t: Pulmonary edema: blast fluid off the alveoli; alert and follows commands
opts.why: Test = fluid in the lungs. Not a bag and not a ventilator.

opts.t: Respiratory arrest
opts.why: Arrest gets a bag.

opts.t: Any trauma chest
opts.why: Trauma takes CPAP off the table.

opts.t: Unconscious with a gag
opts.why: They must follow commands.

q: Adult systolic under 90. Why is that a CPAP stop?

opts.t: Extra chest pressure can drop blood pressure further
opts.why: Adult SBP under 90 is a named veto. 88/60 means no CPAP.

opts.t: Low pressure means they need a cannula at 1 liter
opts.why: Shock is an oxygen reason, but CPAP is still a no.

opts.t: Low pressure means pop the non-rebreather valves off
opts.why: That is a partial rebreather, not a CPAP rule.

opts.t: Low pressure is required before CPAP can start
opts.why: Low pressure is the stop, not the start.

q: Which finding kills CPAP?

opts.t: Cannot follow commands, vomit, trauma, or they want to lie down while short of breath
opts.why: Also hypotension, pneumothorax, face trauma, shock, GI bleed, cannot protect the airway. If they want to lie down, they have given up: bag.

opts.t: Alert, sitting, wet lungs, systolic 110
opts.why: That is a CPAP candidate picture.

opts.t: They say they cannot breathe but still follow commands and sit up
opts.why: Distress plus talking can still be CPAP if the vetoes are absent.

opts.t: Pulse ox 92 percent and they are sitting
opts.why: Hypoxia is a reason, not a veto.

q: Coughing, a little talk, noisy air, grabbing at the throat. What obstruction, and what is done?

opts.t: Mild: hands off, maybe a non-rebreather while they cough
opts.why: Mild still moves air. Load oxygen in case it goes severe.

opts.t: Severe: five back blows and five abdominal thrusts now
opts.why: Talk and cough means it is not the silent severe picture.

opts.t: Unresponsive: start CPR
opts.why: They are still up and moving air.

opts.t: Infant chest thrusts only
opts.why: This is not the infant sequence, and they are still moving air.

q: Silent, blue, choking sign, still up. Adult or child. What sequence?

opts.t: Five back blows, then five abdominal thrusts, repeat
opts.why: AHA now. They do not say Heimlich. Fist above the umbilicus, in and up.

opts.t: Abdominal thrusts only, no backs
opts.why: The 12th book missed backs. The update is 5 and 5.

opts.t: Five backs, then five chest thrusts, like an infant
opts.why: Chest thrusts are the infant half.

opts.t: Hands off and a cannula at 1 liter
opts.why: Severe and awake means hands on.

q: Conscious infant, severe obstruction. What sequence did not change?

opts.t: Support face on the forearm, five backs, sandwich flip, five chest thrusts
opts.why: Infant book is unchanged: 5 back, 5 chest.

opts.t: Five backs, then five abdominal thrusts
opts.why: Abdominal thrusts are adult and child, not infant.

opts.t: Hands off and watch
opts.why: Severe means hands on.

opts.t: Start adult 30 and 2 while they are still awake
opts.why: CPR starts when they go unresponsive.

q: They were choking and now they collapse. Next?

opts.t: On the back and start CPR; compressions still try to pop the object
opts.why: Unresponsive from choke → supine CPR. Not because they already died.

opts.t: Keep abdominal thrusts while they are down
opts.why: Down means CPR.

opts.t: CPAP to blast the object out
opts.why: CPAP is not a choke tool.

opts.t: A nasal airway through the object
opts.why: That does not clear a choke.

q: Dentures while trying to seal a mask?

opts.t: Stable and not in the way: leave them; loose and a problem: take them out
opts.why: Stable dentures can help the seal. Loose ones fall back.

opts.t: Always pull them, even if they are solid
opts.why: Solid ones stay.

opts.t: Always leave them, even if they are loose
opts.why: Loose ones come out.

opts.t: Cut wires for fun on every brace
opts.why: Wires only if they truly block.

q: Smashed, bleeding face. Which pair is true?

opts.t: Suction blood in the airway, pressure on the outside bleed, no nasal airway, no CPAP; oral airway is still OK if they qualify
opts.why: Face trauma: no NPA, no CPAP. OPA is OK if unresponsive and no gag.

opts.t: Nasal airway first, then CPAP
opts.why: Both are banned with face trauma.

opts.t: Skip suction and bag through the blood
opts.why: Blood in the path is suctioned.

opts.t: Oral airway is banned whenever the face is hit
opts.why: OPA is still allowed if they qualify.

q: Adequately breathing. Which finding still gets oxygen?

opts.t: Pulse ox under 94, they say they cannot breathe, or shock signs
opts.why: Need one of those three. Class target stays 94-99.

opts.t: Pulse ox 99, no distress, no shock
opts.why: None of the three means probably no oxygen.

opts.t: Only a sat under 90, never under 94
opts.why: The named cutoff is under 94.

opts.t: Only after a Venturi color is chosen
opts.why: Venturi numbers are not invented here.

q: D cylinder versus H cylinder?

opts.t: D is the small portable; H is the tall one mounted for transport
opts.why: Switch off the little tank onto H in the truck. Exact liters of gas were not given.

opts.t: H is the small portable; D is the tall wall tank
opts.why: Those letters are swapped.

opts.t: Both are the same size and both stay unsecured
opts.why: Sizes differ, and tanks stay secured.

opts.t: D is only for CPAP; H is only for a cannula
opts.why: Both are oxygen tanks, not device-specific.

q: Full tank pressure, then what does the regulator knock it to?

opts.t: About 2,000 psi down to about 40 to 70 psi
opts.why: A car tire is about 30. The flow meter then reads liters per minute.

opts.t: About 300 mmHg down to 10 psi
opts.why: 300 mmHg is a suction vacuum number.

opts.t: About 21 psi down to 6 psi
opts.why: 21% is room air, and 6 is a cannula liter cap.

opts.t: About 90 to 95 psi with no drop
opts.why: 90-95% is a non-rebreather percent, not tank psi.

q: Bourdon gage versus a pressure-compensated flow meter?

opts.t: Bourdon works in any position; pressure-compensated must stay upright
opts.why: Bourdon is for tanks you lay down or strap. Compensated is wall ambulance / hospital.

opts.t: Bourdon must stay upright; pressure-compensated works on its side
opts.why: Those are swapped.

opts.t: Both must stay upright, and both are suction gages
opts.why: These are oxygen flow meters, and Bourdon can lie down.

opts.t: Neither is used on oxygen
opts.why: Both are oxygen flow meters.

q: Why must a cylinder stay in a hand, laid down, strapped, or locked?

opts.t: About 2,000 psi; a broken valve can turn it into a missile
opts.why: Practice as if full. Lay it down when it is not in a hand.

opts.t: About 21 psi; it only stains the floor
opts.why: The danger is the high pressure, not a stain.

opts.t: It is empty at school, so it can stand free
opts.why: Practice as if full even when school tanks are empty.

opts.t: Pin indexing already stops it from falling
opts.why: Pin indexing stops the wrong gas, not a tip-over.

q: What does pin indexing actually stop?

opts.t: Putting the wrong-gas regulator on an oxygen tank
opts.why: Oxygen pins are two holes side by side. Oxygen regulator only on an oxygen tank. Tanks are silver and/or green.

opts.t: A tank tipping over
opts.why: A hand, a strap, or the floor stops a tip.

opts.t: A mask running under 10 liters
opts.why: Flow is a meter setting, not pins.

opts.t: Carbon monoxide binding 250 to 300 times better
opts.why: That bind ratio is a pulse-ox lie, not a pin pattern.

q: Cheyne-Stokes or ataxic after a big head hit. What is likely needed?

opts.t: Ventilate; time with their inhale if they have one; do not match 40 a minute
opts.why: Keep about 10 good breaths a minute for an adult. Good spells plus bad or apnea spells.

opts.t: Hands off because any fast rate is Kussmaul
opts.why: This pair often needs a bag, not a leave-it.

opts.t: CPAP because the face was hit
opts.why: Face or chest trauma kills CPAP.

opts.t: A cannula at 1 liter only
opts.why: They likely need a bag, not a cannula.
